subject: What is the largest model you've used with Stan?

messages.author: 738bba66aa2dab9b
messages.subject: What is the largest model you've used with Stan?
parts:
Hello group,

Obviously the mere dimensionality of a problem doesn't fully determine the speed of convergence of a MCMC. The correlation between the variables, the complexity of the model, etc all play important roles.

That said, I'm trying to get a sense of the order of magnitude of the size of problems that have a chance to be tackled.

Is it sensible to use Stan on a model with hundreds of parameters? Tens of thousands? Millions?

Some of the default behaviors of cmdstan (such as printing each parameter for each sample) suggest that the typical models have at most dozens of parameters. Is that so?

Thanks,
Arthur

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What is the largest model you've used with Stan?
parts:
The examples are misleading because most of them are from
textbooks that have kept things simple and small.

We've fit simple models like IRT with millions of parameters,
but it takes a few hours. We regularly fit all kinds of
models with thousands of parameters.

CmdStan saves each sample (but can be set to thin). We're
thinking about adding something to CmdStan like RStan has
that will let you suppress output for some variables.

If the saved output is too big, it can choke our posterior
analysis tools. But that's a different problem than the
sampler not working. You can still easily do things like
compute posterior means and sd using online algorithms like
Welford's and you can do pretty well at getting wide
intervals (50% intervals require saving half the samples online,
whereas 5% intervals only require saving 5% in memory).

If you want to do logistic regression with L1 regularization
and millions of parameters and billions of sparse training instances,
you'll need to use something more specialized like Vowpal Wabbit.
Of course, there's a problem with summarizing output given their
hashing, but again, that's a different problem than being able to
fit the model.

- Bob

messages.author: 0839befa8a8b7d53
messages.subject: Re: What is the largest model you've used with Stan?
parts:
I think the largest number of parameters I've used in a Stan model is about 30k. It worked just fine.

In fact, sometimes I add parameters by taking out e.g. marginalization and it actually fits better. Earlier this year, I worked a hidden Markov model with gamma latency emissions with lots of censoring, and just estimating the censored values as missing with known constraint lead to slightly better mixing than using the gamma ccdf, even though it added lots of parameters to the posterior.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: What is the largest model you've used with Stan?
parts:
The default for HMC is to estimate a diagonal mass
matrix during warmup. You can override that and have
it estimate a full mass matrix or just take a unit
mass matrix. The default for optimization is to use
L-BFGS which approximates a Hessian using a finite history
of gradients, but never needs to store the whole matrix or
do an inversion.

We haven't found many problems where a dense mass matrix
is helpful.

Feel free to ask on the list about how things work now --- some
of the historical notes are now just that.

- Bob

parts: Thanks! Here's one more question: is there an easy way to use a MAP estimate as a starting point for a chain?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: What is the largest model you've used with Stan?
parts:
It's possible using optimization. It's easier in R/Python than
from the command line.

Having said that, Stan usually converges quickly from diffuse
starting points. Running multiple such chains and getting to
the same end point is a further check that you're really
at convergence.

Also, many models of interest, such as hierarchical models,
do not have posterior modes (density approaches infinity as
hierarchical variance approaches zero and the low-level parameters
approach the hierarchical mean). In those cases, it's possible
to only iterate the L-BFGS solver for optimization a few iterations,
but you're in uncharted waters. Do report back if you go there
and survive and have advice for the rest of us.

- Bob

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: What is the largest model you've used with Stan?
parts:
Hi Richard,

Thanks for clarifying. Do you have any idea why adding parameters for censored values yielded better mixing, compared to integrating out the censored values? Could it be a results of potential differences in numerical stability of the PDF and CDF functions in Stan? E.g., the CDF function normal_cdf_log will default to -Inf for (y-mu)/sigma < 8.25, which may happen for censored values if the model's expected value for said value is well above the censoring threshold (assuming left-censoring in this case) and sigma is not too large. The manual does not state anything about the numerical stability of normal_log, but if it's more stable than the CDF (i.e. it defaults to -Inf for z << 8.25), it might explain things.

Or maybe there's an entirely different explanation for the better mixing you report?

I've been having mixing issues with a model for data that are partly left-censored. In this model I ise the lognormal_cdf_log function to integrate out censored values.. It'd be great if using the PDF (effectively truncated by the constraints on the parameter) could help there, though it will be pain to code as the observations in the data have been censored at different values (hopefully we'll be able to use vectors of values for parameters constraints in the near future).

Thanks,

Luc
